codes.label: Parent's own wishes and dignity
codes.definition: The parent's preferences about where and how they live, who helps with intimate care, and how much autonomy they keep should be asked directly and given real weight, even with cognitive decline.

codes.label: Medical needs and prognosis
codes.definition: The parent's actual medical and functional needs, such as mobility, transfers, medication, supervision, and whether care is skilled or basic, and the likely recovery or decline trajectory, determine what level of care is truly required.

codes.label: Progression and changing needs over time
codes.definition: Because recovery or decline is unpredictable, the chosen arrangement should be judged by how well it handles a worse or longer future, including later stages like wandering or 24-hour supervision, and whether it avoids a second disruptive move.

codes.label: Safety and fall risk
codes.definition: Recent falls and cognitive decline signal an immediate safety problem, so each option must be weighed by the supervision, emergency response, and fall prevention it can realistically provide.

codes.label: Home safety and modifications
codes.definition: Whichever house is used needs to be assessed for stairs, bathroom access, grab bars, bedroom location, and night-time supervision, along with the cost and feasibility of adapting it.

codes.label: Funding runway and what comes after
codes.definition: The parent's savings cover care for only a finite time (about a year for aides, about four years for the facility), so the plan must account for what happens when money runs out, including a possible hidden backstop on the caregiver.

codes.label: Public benefits and insurance eligibility
codes.definition: Medicaid, Medicare, veterans' benefits, long-term care insurance, waiver programs and local agencies may offset costs, and rules on eligibility and how assets are treated vary by option.

codes.label: Legal and financial documentation
codes.definition: Whether power of attorney, healthcare proxy, advance directives, and a current will are in place determines who can make decisions and manage money, and these are time-sensitive, especially with dementia.

codes.label: Professional guidance and elder-law advice
codes.definition: Consulting doctors, geriatric care managers, social workers, or elder-law and financial professionals can test assumptions and clarify options before committing.

codes.label: Caregiver burnout and personal wellbeing
codes.definition: Sustained hands-on caregiving risks exhaustion, isolation, and health and mental-health costs for the caregiver, which can eventually undermine the care the parent receives.

codes.label: Caregiver's job and career consequences
codes.definition: Working full time while caregiving, or taking unpaid leave, can cost income, advancement, retirement contributions, licensure or clinical currency, and re-entry prospects beyond the immediate lost wages.

codes.label: Job protection and leave options
codes.definition: Whether leave is legally protected or job-guaranteed, whether any income replacement exists, and whether remote or part-time work is possible determine how risky the leave option really is.

codes.label: Caregiver's own financial runway
codes.definition: The caregiver must calculate how long they can cover rent, bills, insurance, and retirement savings on reduced or no income, including costs of maintaining two households.

codes.label: Spouse and household strain
codes.definition: A spouse's willingness, availability, and frequent absence determine whether a home arrangement is a shared plan or a solo burden, and it changes marital and household routines and privacy.

codes.label: Sole caregiver with no one to share the load
codes.definition: Having no sibling or backup caregiver on site means no relief for emergencies, overnight needs, illness, or respite, so single-point-of-failure risk should be weighed and a backup plan identified.

codes.label: Sibling's offer of support
codes.definition: A distant sibling's emotional support does not reduce daily workload, so it should be converted into specific commitments such as money, research, paperwork, visits, or respite coverage.

codes.label: Reversibility and flexibility
codes.definition: Options differ in how easily they can be undone or adjusted, so choosing the more reversible path, a trial period, or checkpoints for reassessment can preserve future choices.

codes.label: Hybrid and middle-path options
codes.definition: Alternatives such as part-time aides, adult day programs, respite stays, a phased plan, or partial leave can soften an all-or-nothing choice and let the family test assumptions.

codes.label: Quality and reliability of paid care
codes.definition: Hired aides or facilities vary in turnover, training, staffing ratios, and dementia capability, and cannot fully replace a family member's attentiveness, so local availability and vetting matter.

codes.label: Managing paid care as a job
codes.definition: Hiring aides means scheduling, supervising, and resolving conflicts with a rotating team, which is its own ongoing burden and cost of the hire-out option.

codes.label: Facility quality and fit
codes.definition: Touring a facility and checking staffing, memory-care capability, fall practices, inspection records, and whether it can handle higher levels of care determines whether it is a good long-term setting.

codes.label: Familiar surroundings and disruption
codes.definition: Moving someone with dementia or a stroke survivor away from familiar surroundings can increase confusion and loss of identity, so each option's disorientation and effect on routine and social ties should be compared.

codes.label: Social connection and quality of life
codes.definition: Facilities may offer peers, activities, and professional staff while home settings offer familiarity and family love but possibly isolation, so quality of daily life differs by option.

codes.label: Proximity and ease of monitoring
codes.definition: Distance affects how often the caregiver can visit, attend appointments, and respond to emergencies, so a nearby facility or a nearby move changes oversight and sustainability.

codes.label: Parent-child relationship and role shift
codes.definition: Becoming a caregiver can turn a child into a nurse or supervisor, strain the bond, and revive old family dynamics, so the ability to remain a son or daughter and preserve the relationship matters.

codes.label: Caregiver's clinical expertise
codes.definition: A caregiver's professional training can improve rehabilitation and judging of aide quality, but may also blur roles, add second-guessing, and make it hard to simply be family.

codes.label: Caregiver's personal life and relationships
codes.definition: Relocating or becoming a full-time caregiver affects friendships, dating prospects, social network, housing, and the kind of life the caregiver wants to build.

codes.label: Housing and logistics costs of relocating
codes.definition: Breaking or subletting a lease, storing belongings, maintaining or selling the parent's home, and running two households add expenses and hassles that should be budgeted.

codes.label: Early-recovery window
codes.definition: The first weeks and months after a stroke are when recovery is most malleable and dependence patterns form, so who provides early help may shape long-term independence.

codes.label: Long-term planning beyond the immediate decision
codes.definition: The crisis is a chance to plan for where the parent will live and be cared for in the years ahead, including exit triggers, so the choice does not drift into an open-ended commitment.

codes.label: Regret and values reflection
codes.definition: Imagining years ahead which choice could be explained without guilt or resentment helps clarify what kind of caregiver one wants to be and separates values from obligation.

codes.label: Distinguishing real support from nominal support
codes.definition: Support that costs the giver nothing day to day should be separated from commitments that actually share the burden before it is counted as a resource.

codes.label: Spare-room arrangement drifting into permanence
codes.definition: A temporary home arrangement tends to become permanent by default and is hard to undo, so weighing the asymmetric cost of being wrong in each direction matters.

codes.label: Other dependents' needs
codes.definition: Caring for the parent can reduce the time, money, and attention available to children or other people who depend on the caregiver, so the whole household's needs must be weighed.

codes.label: Driving and transportation
codes.definition: Falls and cognitive decline may mean the parent can no longer drive, so each option should be judged by how he would reach medical appointments, therapy, and errands.

codes.label: Tax implications of caregiving
codes.definition: Each arrangement may carry different tax consequences, such as deductions or credits for care expenses, the treatment of aide payments, and effects on the parent's taxable income.

codes.label: Community and caregiver support networks
codes.definition: Local caregiver support groups, stroke or dementia survivor resources, and respite programs can lighten the load and make either option more sustainable.

codes.label: Precedent for the caregiver's own future care
codes.definition: How the caregiver handles this period models expectations about their own later-life care and what they can reasonably ask of family, so the choice has implications beyond the present.
